title: Redox Reactions

toc.title: 5.1 Classical and electronic concepts of oxidation and reduction; oxidation number
5.2 Balancing redox equations by the oxidation-number and ion-electron methods; applications

html:
Redox reactions carry about one question in the paper (our estimate from the MEC topic list), but oxidation numbers and balanced redox equations are used again in electrochemistry, volumetric analysis (permanganate and dichromate titrations), metallurgy and the chemistry of non-metals. The question is usually an oxidation number (often a tricky one such as Fe₃O₄, CrO₅ or S₄O₆²⁻), identifying the oxidant, reductant or a disproportionation, or a coefficient or mole ratio from a balanced redox equation.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • Oxidation = loss of electrons (increase in oxidation number); reduction = gain of electrons (decrease). The oxidising agent is reduced; the reducing agent is oxidised.
  • The oxidation-number rules, and the exceptions: O is −1 in peroxides, −½ in superoxides, +2 in OF₂; H is −1 in metal hydrides; F is always −1.
  • Fractional and "impossible" values: Fe₃O₄ +8/3, S₄O₆²⁻ +2.5; peroxide bridges keep CrO₅ and H₂S₂O₈ at +6.
  • Disproportionation (one element both oxidised and reduced) and its reverse, comproportionation.
  • Balancing by oxidation number and by ion-electron (half-reaction) methods, in acid and in base.
  • n-factor: moles react in the inverse ratio of their electron changes (KMnO₄ 5 in acid, K₂Cr₂O₇ 6).

5.1 Classical and electronic concepts of oxidation and reduction; oxidation number

The classical concept

Oxidation is Reduction is Example
addition of oxygen removal of oxygen 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO (Mg oxidised); CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O (CuO reduced)
removal of hydrogen addition of hydrogen H₂S + Cl₂ → 2HCl + S (H₂S oxidised, Cl₂ reduced)
addition of an electronegative element removal of an electronegative element 2FeCl₂ + Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃ (FeCl₂ oxidised)
removal of an electropositive element addition of an electropositive element 2KI + H₂O₂ → 2KOH + I₂ (KI oxidised: K removed from I)

The classical definitions cannot handle reactions with no oxygen or hydrogen at all, such as Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu. The electronic concept covers everything.

The electronic concept

Oxidation and reduction (electronic)

Oxidation is the loss of electrons by an atom, ion or molecule (de-electronation); reduction is the gain of electrons (electronation). An oxidising agent (oxidant) accepts electrons and is itself reduced; a reducing agent (reductant) donates electrons and is itself oxidised. The two always happen together — a redox reaction.

In Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, the half-reactions are Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ (oxidation) and Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (reduction). Zinc is the reducing agent; Cu²⁺ is the oxidising agent.

OIL RIG

Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons). And the agent is the opposite of what happens to it: the oxidising agent gets reduced.

Oxidation number

Oxidation number

The oxidation number (oxidation state) of an atom is the charge it would carry if every bond in the compound were ionic, the shared electrons being given to the more electronegative atom. It can be positive, negative, zero or fractional (an average).

Rule Exceptions to remember
An element in the free state: 0 (Na, H₂, O₃, P₄, S₈) —
A monatomic ion: its charge (Na⁺ +1, Cl⁻ −1, Al³⁺ +3) —
Fluorine: always −1 none — it is the most electronegative element
Oxygen: −2 peroxides (H₂O₂, Na₂O₂, BaO₂) −1; superoxides (KO₂) −½; OF₂ +2; O₂F₂ +1
Hydrogen: +1 metal hydrides (NaH, CaH₂, LiAlH₄) −1
Group 1 metals +1, group 2 metals +2 in compounds —
Sum of all oxidation numbers = 0 for a molecule, = the charge for an ion —

In terms of oxidation numbers, oxidation is an increase and reduction a decrease. A reaction in which no oxidation number changes (neutralisation, precipitation, most double decompositions) is not a redox reaction.

Element Oxidation numbers worth knowing
Mn KMnO₄ +7, K₂MnO₄ +6, MnO₂ +4, Mn²⁺ +2
Cr K₂Cr₂O₇ and K₂CrO₄ +6, Cr³⁺ +3, CrO₅ +6 (two peroxide groups)
S H₂S −2, S 0, S₂O₃²⁻ +2 (average), S₄O₆²⁻ +2.5 (average), SO₂ +4, H₂SO₄ +6, H₂S₂O₈ +6
N NH₃ −3, N₂H₄ −2, NH₂OH −1, N₂ 0, N₂O +1, NO +2, HNO₂ +3, NO₂ +4, HNO₃ +5, HN₃ −⅓
C CH₄ −4, CH₃OH −2, HCHO 0, HCOOH +2, CO +2, CO₂ +4
P H₃PO₂ +1, H₃PO₃ +3, H₃PO₄ +5
Cl HCl −1, HOCl +1, HClO₂ +3, HClO₃ +5, HClO₄ +7
Fe Fe₃O₄ +8/3 (average; really one Fe²⁺ and two Fe³⁺), [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ +2, [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻ +3
Others OsO₄ +8 (the highest in any stable compound), Ni(CO)₄ 0, NH₄NO₃: N −3 and +5
When the simple sum gives an impossible answer

A sum that exceeds the group number (Cr > +6, S > +6) means the formula hides a peroxide (–O–O–) link, whose oxygens are −1. CrO₅ by simple arithmetic gives +10, but its structure has two peroxide groups and one ordinary oxygen: x + 4(−1) + (−2) = 0, so x = +6. Fractional values (Fe₃O₄, S₄O₆²⁻, HN₃) are averages over atoms in different environments.

Oxidation numbers by the rules

Problem. Find the oxidation number of (i) S in H₂S₂O₈ (one peroxide link), (ii) N in NH₂OH, (iii) C in C₃O₂.

Solution. (i) 2(+1) + 2x + 6(−2) + 2(−1) = 0 → 2x = 12 → +6 (not +7, which the naive sum gives). (ii) x + 2(+1) + (−2) + (+1) = 0 → −1. (iii) 3x + 2(−2) = 0 → +4/3 (an average).

Types of redox reaction

Type What happens Examples
Combination elements or compounds join C + O₂ → CO₂; 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl
Decomposition a compound breaks up 2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂; 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂
Displacement a more reactive element displaces a less reactive one Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu; Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂
Disproportionation the same element is both oxidised and reduced 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂; Cl₂ + 2NaOH (cold, dilute) → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O; 3Cl₂ + 6NaOH (hot) → 5NaCl + NaClO₃ + 3H₂O; 2Cu⁺ → Cu + Cu²⁺; 3HNO₂ → HNO₃ + 2NO + H₂O
Comproportionation two oxidation states of one element meet in the middle 2H₂S + SO₂ → 3S + 2H₂O

Who can do what? An element in its highest oxidation state can only gain electrons — it can act only as an oxidising agent (KMnO₄, K₂Cr₂O₇, HNO₃). In its lowest state it can act only as a reducing agent (H₂S, NH₃, I⁻). In an intermediate state it can act as both (H₂O₂, SO₂, HNO₂, NO₂⁻) — which is also why such species can disproportionate.

5.2 Balancing redox equations by the oxidation-number and ion-electron methods; applications

The oxidation-number method

  1. Write the skeleton equation and the oxidation numbers of every atom; pick out the atoms whose oxidation numbers change.
  2. Find the increase per formula unit of the reductant and the decrease per formula unit of the oxidant (multiply by the number of such atoms in the formula).
  3. Multiply so that the total increase equals the total decrease.
  4. Balance the other atoms by inspection — the spectator ions first, then H with H₂O (or H⁺/OH⁻ in ionic equations), and check O last.
Oxidation-number method: KMnO₄ with HCl

Problem. Balance KMnO₄ + HCl → KCl + MnCl₂ + Cl₂ + H₂O.

Solution. Mn: +7 → +2, a decrease of 5 per Mn. Cl: −1 → 0, an increase of 1 per Cl, so 2 per Cl₂ formed. Equalise: 2 Mn (decrease 10) and 5 Cl₂ (increase 10): 2KMnO₄ + ? HCl → 2KCl + 2MnCl₂ + 5Cl₂ + ? H₂O. Chlorine on the right = 2 + 4 + 10 = 16, so 16 HCl; hydrogen 16 → 8 H₂O; oxygen 8 = 8. ✓ 2KMnO₄ + 16HCl → 2KCl + 2MnCl₂ + 5Cl₂ + 8H₂O.

The ion-electron (half-reaction) method

  1. Split the ionic equation into an oxidation and a reduction half.
  2. In each half balance the atoms other than O and H.
  3. Acidic medium: balance O by adding H₂O to the side short of O, then balance H by adding H⁺ to the other side. Basic medium: balance as if acidic, then add as many OH⁻ to both sides as there are H⁺; combine H⁺ + OH⁻ into H₂O and cancel water.
  4. Balance charge by adding electrons.
  5. Multiply the halves so that electrons lost = electrons gained; add and cancel.
Ion-electron method in acid: dichromate and hydrogen sulphide

Problem. Balance Cr₂O₇²⁻ + H₂S → Cr³⁺ + S in acidic solution.

Solution. Reduction: Cr₂O₇²⁻ → 2Cr³⁺; add 7H₂O on the right and 14H⁺ on the left; charge: left +12, right +6, so add 6e⁻ on the left: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O. Oxidation: H₂S → S + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻. Multiply it by 3 and add, cancelling 6H⁺: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 3H₂S + 8H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 3S + 7H₂O. Check charge: −2 + 8 = +6 = 2(+3). ✓

Ion-electron method in base: chromium(III) hydroxide and hypochlorite

Problem. Balance Cr(OH)₃ + ClO⁻ → CrO₄²⁻ + Cl⁻ in basic solution.

Solution. Oxidation (as if acidic): Cr(OH)₃ + H₂O → CrO₄²⁻ + 5H⁺ + 3e⁻. Reduction: ClO⁻ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cl⁻ + H₂O. Multiply by 2 and 3 to equalise six electrons and add: 2Cr(OH)₃ + 3ClO⁻ → 2CrO₄²⁻ + 3Cl⁻ + 4H⁺ + H₂O. Add 4OH⁻ to both sides (4H⁺ + 4OH⁻ = 4H₂O): 2Cr(OH)₃ + 3ClO⁻ + 4OH⁻ → 2CrO₄²⁻ + 3Cl⁻ + 5H₂O. Charge: −7 = −7. ✓

The n-factor shortcut

The n-factor of an oxidant or reductant is the number of electrons it gains or loses per formula unit. In any redox reaction the moles that react are in the inverse ratio of the n-factors — the same idea gives equivalent weights in Unit 8.

Reagent and change n-factor
MnO₄⁻ → Mn²⁺ (acidic) 5
MnO₄⁻ → MnO₂ (neutral or weakly basic) 3
MnO₄⁻ → MnO₄²⁻ (strongly basic) 1
Cr₂O₇²⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ (acidic) 6
Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ 1
C₂O₄²⁻ → 2CO₂ 2
FeC₂O₄ → Fe³⁺ + 2CO₂ 1 + 2 = 3
H₂O₂ → O₂ (as reductant) or → H₂O (as oxidant) 2
2S₂O₃²⁻ → S₄O₆²⁻ 1 per S₂O₃²⁻
I₂ → 2I⁻ 2

So one MnO₄⁻ (n = 5) oxidises five Fe²⁺ (n = 1) in acid, and one Cr₂O₇²⁻ (n = 6) oxidises six: MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O and Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 6Fe²⁺ + 14H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 6Fe³⁺ + 7H₂O. In acidified permanganate–oxalate, 2MnO₄⁻ + 5C₂O₄²⁻ + 16H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 10CO₂ + 8H₂O, ten electrons change hands.

Check a coefficient question without balancing

For "what is x?" questions, first equalise the electrons (n-factors), which fixes the coefficients of the oxidant and reductant at once; then count O to fix H₂O, and H (or the charge) to fix H⁺. The charge check — left side total equals right side total — catches most slips.

Applications of redox reactions

Field Redox at work
Metallurgy ores are reduced to metals: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂ (blast furnace); Cr₂O₃ + 2Al → 2Cr + Al₂O₃ (aluminothermy)
Electrochemistry cells and batteries: oxidation at the anode, reduction at the cathode (Unit 10)
Titrations permanganometry, dichrometry, iodometry and iodimetry (Units 8 and 22)
Bleaching Cl₂ bleaches by oxidation (HOCl releases [O]) — permanent; SO₂ bleaches by reduction (nascent hydrogen) — temporary
Corrosion rusting is the oxidation of iron by O₂ and water
Biology photosynthesis (CO₂ reduced) and respiration (glucose oxidised)
Industry Ostwald process (NH₃ oxidised to HNO₃), contact process (SO₂ → SO₃), chlorine water treatment
Breath tests orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ is reduced to green Cr³⁺ by ethanol

Formula and fact sheet

Item Rule
Oxidation loss of e⁻; increase in oxidation number; addition of O or removal of H (classical)
Reduction gain of e⁻; decrease in oxidation number
Oxidising agent gets reduced (accepts e⁻); reducing agent gets oxidised
Sum of oxidation numbers 0 for a molecule; the charge for an ion
Fixed values F −1; group 1 +1; group 2 +2; O −2 (except peroxide −1, superoxide −½, OF₂ +2); H +1 (−1 in metal hydrides)
Balancing in acid O with H₂O, H with H⁺, charge with e⁻
Balancing in base balance as acid, then add OH⁻ to both sides to remove H⁺
n-factor rule moles react in the inverse ratio of n-factors
Must-know balanced equations
MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O
Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 6Fe²⁺ + 14H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 6Fe³⁺ + 7H₂O
2MnO₄⁻ + 5C₂O₄²⁻ + 16H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 10CO₂ + 8H₂O
3Cu + 8HNO₃ (dilute) → 3Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO + 4H₂O
Cu + 4HNO₃ (concentrated) → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO₂ + 2H₂O
2KMnO₄ + 16HCl → 2KCl + 2MnCl₂ + 5Cl₂ + 8H₂O
2S₂O₃²⁻ + I₂ → S₄O₆²⁻ + 2I⁻

Chapter summary

  • Classical: oxidation = addition of O or an electronegative element, removal of H or an electropositive element; reduction the reverse.
  • Electronic: oxidation = loss of electrons, reduction = gain; the oxidant is reduced and the reductant oxidised; both always occur together.
  • Oxidation number rules: free element 0; F −1; O −2 except peroxides (−1), superoxides (−½) and OF₂ (+2); H +1 except metal hydrides (−1); the sum equals the charge.
  • Watch the traps: Fe₃O₄ +8/3, S₄O₆²⁻ +2.5, CrO₅ and H₂S₂O₈ +6 (peroxide links), OsO₄ +8, NH₄NO₃ −3 and +5.
  • Highest oxidation state → only an oxidant; lowest → only a reductant; intermediate → both, and able to disproportionate (H₂O₂, Cl₂ in alkali, Cu⁺, HNO₂).
  • Balancing: equalise the total change in oxidation number, or add half-reactions after balancing O with H₂O, H with H⁺ (OH⁻ in base) and charge with electrons.
  • n-factors: MnO₄⁻ 5 (acid), 3 (neutral), 1 (strong base); Cr₂O₇²⁻ 6; moles react in the inverse ratio of n-factors.

Practice questions

Set A — Recall (20 questions)

  1. In terms of electrons, oxidation isaloss of electronsbgain of electronscgain of protonsdloss of neutrons
  2. In the classical concept, which change is a reduction?aaddition of oxygenbremoval of hydrogencremoval of oxygendaddition of an electronegative element
  3. An oxidising agent is a substance thataloses electronsbis itself oxidisedcdonates hydrogendgains electrons and is itself reduced
  4. The oxidation number of an element in its free (uncombined) state isa+1b0c−1dequal to its valency
  5. The oxidation number of oxygen in H₂O₂ isa−2b−½c−1d+1
  6. The oxidation number of hydrogen in NaH isa−1b+1c0d+2
  7. The oxidation number of manganese in KMnO₄ isa+6b+7c+5d+4
  8. The oxidation number of chromium in K₂Cr₂O₇ isa+3b+7c+12d+6
  9. The oxidation number of oxygen in OF₂ isa−2b−1c+2d0
  10. A reaction in which the same element is both oxidised and reduced is calledadisproportionationbdisplacementccombinationdneutralisation
  11. The oxidation number of fluorine in all its compounds isa+1b0c+1 or −1d−1
  12. In the reaction Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, the reducing agent isaCu²⁺bZncZn²⁺dCu
  13. The oxidation number of osmium in OsO₄, the highest found in any stable compound, isa+8b+7c+6d+4
  14. Oxygen has the oxidation number −½ inaH₂O₂bBaO₂cKO₂dOF₂
  15. Which of these can act only as a reducing agent?aSO₂bH₂ScH₂SO₄dS
  16. Which of these can act only as an oxidising agent?aH₂O₂bSO₂cHNO₂dKMnO₄
  17. The oxidation number of nitrogen in HNO₃ isa+5b+3c+4d−3
  18. In the ion-electron method for an acidic solution, oxygen atoms are balanced by addingaOH⁻ ionsbO₂ moleculescelectronsdH₂O molecules
  19. The rusting of iron is an example ofathe reduction of ironbneutralisationcthe oxidation of irondthe decomposition of iron
  20. In the reaction 2FeCl₂ + Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃, iron(II) chloride isareduced, as chlorine is removedboxidised, as an electronegative element is addedcneither oxidised nor reduceddoxidised, as hydrogen is removed
Answers and explanations — Set A

1. (a) — Oxidation is loss of electrons (OIL RIG); gain of electrons is reduction.

2. (c) — Removal of oxygen is reduction (CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O). The other three are classical oxidations.

3. (d) — An oxidant takes electrons from something else and is reduced in doing so.

4. (b) — Atoms of one element share bonding electrons equally, so each is 0 (H₂, O₂, P₄, S₈, Na).

5. (c) — 2(+1) + 2x = 0 → x = −1 (a peroxide). −½ is the superoxide value.

6. (a) — In a metal hydride hydrogen is the more electronegative partner: Na⁺H⁻.

7. (b) — +1 + x + 4(−2) = 0 → x = +7.

8. (d) — 2(+1) + 2x + 7(−2) = 0 → 2x = 12 → x = +6 for each Cr. Option (c) is the total for both Cr atoms.

9. (c) — Fluorine is more electronegative, so each F is −1 and O must be +2.

10. (a) — Disproportionation, e.g. 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂ (O: −1 → −2 and 0).

11. (d) — Fluorine, the most electronegative element, is −1 in every compound.

12. (b) — Zn loses two electrons (0 → +2), so it is the reducing agent; Cu²⁺ is the oxidising agent.

13. (a) — x + 4(−2) = 0 → x = +8. Osmium in OsO₄ and ruthenium in RuO₄ reach +8, the highest oxidation number in stable compounds.

14. (c) — In KO₂ the superoxide ion O₂⁻ carries −1 over two O atoms: −½ each. BaO₂ and H₂O₂ are peroxides (−1).

15. (b) — Sulphur at −2, its lowest state, can only lose electrons. SO₂ (+4) and S (0) can go up or down; H₂SO₄ (+6) can only go down.

16. (d) — Mn in KMnO₄ is +7, its maximum, so it can only gain electrons. H₂O₂, SO₂ and HNO₂ are in intermediate states and can act both ways.

17. (a) — +1 + x + 3(−2) = 0 → x = +5.

18. (d) — Water supplies O; H⁺ then balances the hydrogen. OH⁻ is used only when converting to a basic medium.

19. (c) — Iron goes from 0 to +3 in hydrated Fe₂O₃ (rust) — it is oxidised; oxygen is reduced.

20. (b) — Adding an electronegative element (Cl) is oxidation in the classical sense; electronically Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻.

Set B — Understanding (13 questions)

  1. The oxidation number of iron in Fe₃O₄ isa+2b+3c+8/3d+4/3
  2. The average oxidation number of sulphur in the tetrathionate ion S₄O₆²⁻ isa+2.5b+2c+3d+6
  3. The oxidation number of chromium in CrO₅, which contains two peroxide groups, isa+10b+5c+8d+6
  4. In the reaction Cl₂ + 2NaOH (cold, dilute) → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O, chlorine isaonly oxidisedbboth oxidised and reducedconly reduceddunchanged in oxidation number
  5. Which of the following is NOT a redox reaction?aNaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂ObZn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂c2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂dCuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O
  6. H₂O₂ can act both as an oxidising agent and as a reducing agent becauseait contains hydrogenbit is a liquidcits oxygen is at −1, between −2 and 0dit is a strong acid
  7. In H₂S + Cl₂ → 2HCl + S, the substance oxidised isaCl₂bHClcSdH₂S
  8. The oxidation numbers of the two nitrogen atoms in NH₄NO₃ area+1 and +5b−3 and +5c+3 and −5d0 and +2
  9. In acidic solution MnO₄⁻ is reduced to Mn²⁺. The number of electrons gained per MnO₄⁻ ion isa3b1c5d7
  10. In which compound is the oxidation number of carbon zero?aHCHObCH₃OHcHCOOHdCO₂
  11. When Cr₂O₇²⁻ is reduced to Cr³⁺ in acid, the number of electrons gained per Cr₂O₇²⁻ ion isa3b6c2d12
  12. Which reaction is a comproportionation, the reverse of disproportionation?a2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂bCl₂ + 2OH⁻ → Cl⁻ + OCl⁻ + H₂Oc3HNO₂ → HNO₃ + 2NO + H₂Od2H₂S + SO₂ → 3S + 2H₂O
  13. Sulphur dioxide bleaches by ___ and chlorine bleaches by ___.areduction; oxidationboxidation; reductioncoxidation; oxidationdreduction; reduction
Answers and explanations — Set B

1. (c) — 3x + 4(−2) = 0 → x = +8/3, an average: Fe₃O₄ is really FeO·Fe₂O₃, one Fe²⁺ and two Fe³⁺.

2. (a) — 4x + 6(−2) = −2 → 4x = 10 → x = +2.5 (an average of two S at +5 and two at 0).

3. (d) — x + 4(−1) + (−2) = 0 → x = +6. The naive sum with every O at −2 gives +10, beyond chromium's maximum of +6.

4. (b) — Cl goes from 0 to −1 in NaCl (reduced) and from 0 to +1 in NaClO (oxidised): disproportionation.

5. (a) — Neutralisation: Na +1, O −2, H +1, Cl −1 on both sides — no oxidation number changes.

6. (c) — Oxygen at −1 can be reduced to −2 (H₂O) or oxidised to 0 (O₂).

7. (d) — S goes from −2 in H₂S to 0: H₂S is oxidised (it loses hydrogen); Cl₂ is reduced.

8. (b) — NH₄⁺: x + 4 = +1 → −3; NO₃⁻: x − 6 = −1 → +5.

9. (c) — +7 → +2 is a gain of 5 electrons: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O.

10. (a) — HCHO: x + 2(+1) + (−2) = 0 → 0. CH₃OH −2, HCOOH +2, CO₂ +4.

11. (b) — Each Cr goes +6 → +3 (3 electrons) and there are two Cr atoms: 6 electrons.

12. (d) — S at −2 (H₂S) and +4 (SO₂) both end at 0. Options (a), (b) and (c) are disproportionations.

13. (a) — SO₂ + 2H₂O → H₂SO₄ + 2[H]: the nascent hydrogen reduces the dye (temporary bleaching). Cl₂ + H₂O → HCl + HOCl, and HOCl gives [O], which oxidises the dye (permanent).

Set C — Application (9 questions)

  1. In the balanced equation a Cu + b HNO₃ (dilute) → a Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO + 4H₂O, a and b area1, 4b3, 8c3, 6d2, 8
  2. In the balanced equation MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + x H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + y H₂O, x and y area4, 8b8, 8c16, 8d8, 4
  3. The number of moles of KMnO₄ needed to oxidise 1 mol of Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ in acidic solution isa0.2b5c1d0.5
  4. The number of moles of K₂Cr₂O₇ needed to oxidise 1 mol of ferrous oxalate, FeC₂O₄, completely in acidic solution (Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ and C₂O₄²⁻ → CO₂) isa1b1/6c1/2d3
  5. The total number of electrons transferred in 2MnO₄⁻ + 5C₂O₄²⁻ + 16H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 10CO₂ + 8H₂O isa5b2c16d10
  6. In neutral or faintly alkaline solution MnO₄⁻ oxidises I⁻ to IO₃⁻ and is itself reduced to MnO₂. The number of moles of MnO₄⁻ that react with 1 mol of I⁻ isa1b2c3d6
  7. The oxidation number of phosphorus in hypophosphorous acid, H₃PO₂ (one OH group and two P–H bonds), isa+1b+3c+5d−1
  8. In the balanced equation Cr₂O₇²⁻ + x Fe²⁺ + y H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + x Fe³⁺ + 7H₂O, x and y area3, 14b6, 7c6, 14d2, 14
  9. In hot alkali, 3Cl₂ + 6OH⁻ → 5Cl⁻ + ClO₃⁻ + 3H₂O. The ratio of chlorine atoms reduced to chlorine atoms oxidised isa5 : 1b1 : 5c3 : 1d1 : 1
